nameStory: The chestnut clam gets its name from its rich, warm brown shell color that closely resembles the glossy mahogany-brown hue of a fresh chestnut. When you hold one up to the light, that deep reddish-brown coloration is unmistakable – like nature's own polished wood finish.
description: The chestnut clam is a small, thick-shelled marine clam that lives buried in sandy and muddy ocean bottoms along New England's coast. These sturdy little bivalves have distinctively rounded, plump shells that feel surprisingly heavy for their size. They typically grow to about 1-2 inches across, with a glossy brown exterior that can range from light chestnut to deep chocolate brown. Like other clams, they're filter feeders that spend their lives partially buried in sediment, extending a siphon up to the surface to draw in water and tiny food particles.

idTips.label: Shell Color
idTips.description: Rich chestnut to chocolate brown exterior that feels smooth and glossy when wet, often with a slight reddish tint that catches the light

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Distinctly rounded and plump profile, almost triangular when viewed from the side, feeling thick and solid in your palm

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Typically 1-2 inches across, fitting comfortably in your hand but feeling surprisingly weighty for such a small shell

idTips.label: Shell Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, glossy surface when fresh with fine growth rings that you can feel with your fingertip, becoming duller when weathered

idTips.label: Shell Thickness
idTips.description: Notably thick and sturdy walls that won't crack easily under gentle pressure, unlike many thin-shelled clams

habitat: Chestnut clams live in sandy and muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters, typically in depths of 6-60 feet from the low tide zone to the subtidal zone. You'll most commonly find their empty shells washed up on sandy beaches after storms, or spot live specimens in tide pools and shallow bays with soft sediments. They prefer areas with good water circulation where they can filter-feed effectively.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells often wash ashore after spring storms, appearing glossy and richly colored on the beach. Live clams become more active as water temperatures rise.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for beachcombing their shells, which appear bright and well-preserved. Live specimens can occasionally be found in shallow tide pools during very low tides.
seasonality.fall: Storm-tossed shells frequently appear on beaches after autumn nor'easters. The brown coloration stands out beautifully against wet sand.
seasonality.winter: Shells continue washing ashore but may appear more weathered and faded. Live clams remain buried deeper in sediment during cold months.

funFact: Chestnut clams can live for over 100 years, with some specimens reaching 150+ years old – you might be holding a shell that was alive when the Civil War began, quietly filtering water on the same seafloor for more than a century!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with quahog clam shells, but chestnut clams are much smaller, rounder, and have that distinctive glossy brown color instead of the quahog's grayish-white exterior. Remember: if it's chestnut brown and fits in your palm, it's likely a chestnut clam.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "chestnut clams," they're not closely related to the more familiar quahogs, steamers, or other common edible clams – they belong to an ancient family called astarte clams that have been around for millions of years with relatively little change.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus in New England waters, chestnut clams are most similar to other astarte clam family members, but they're distinguished by their larger size and distinctive brown coloration. Other astarte clams in the region tend to be smaller and have more muted, grayish colors rather than the rich chestnut brown that makes this species so recognizable.
